gen.1.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Genesis 1
gen.1.text:
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. The first verse of the Bible gives us a summary of the whole chapter. It teaches us: (1) The existence of God before the world and before time. 'In the beginning God'—God was before all things, and is the cause of all things. (2) The creation of the world by God. He made it, and made it out of nothing. There was no pre-existing matter from which it was formed; God spoke, and it was done. (3) The inclusion of all things in 'the heavens and the earth.' There is no part of the creation that is not here included.

The six days of creation reveal a God who works in an orderly progression: light before life, separation before fullness, structure before beauty. Each act is pronounced 'good.' This is the declaration of a Creator who finds satisfaction in His work and pronounces it fit for its purpose. On the sixth day, 'very good'—the pinnacle, the creature made in His own image.
gen.1.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

gen.2.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Genesis 2
gen.2.text:
The seventh day is sanctified—set apart for rest and worship. It is given a different status than the other six: God rested and blessed this day. The Sabbath is not an invention of Moses or a Jewish peculiarity; it is woven into the fabric of creation itself. One day in seven belongs to God.

The second account of creation focuses on man's unique status. The breath of life breathed by God into Adam's nostrils is not the same act as the creation of the animals—it is a personal, intimate bestowal of the image of God. Man is unique among all creatures: made from the earth, yet animated by the divine breath; mortal in origin, yet alive with the life of God.
gen.2.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

gen.3.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Genesis 3
gen.3.text:
The temptation of Eve follows a consistent pattern that we recognize throughout Scripture and in our own experience: (1) Doubt of God's word—'Did God actually say?' The first attack is on the authority of God's revelation. (2) Denial of God's judgment—'You will not surely die.' The enemy minimizes consequences. (3) Defamation of God's character—'God knows that when you eat... you will be like God.' The suggestion is that God is holding something back.

The fall is not simply a moral failure; it is a theological one. Adam and Eve chose to be their own judges of good and evil, placing themselves in the seat that belongs to God alone. The consequences are immediate and comprehensive: guilt, shame, broken fellowship with God, conflict between man and woman, and the cursing of the ground.
gen.3.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

psa.1.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Psalm 1
psa.1.text:
The first Psalm serves as a preface to the whole book, setting before us two contrasting ways—the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. It is both a description and a prescription: here is what the blessed life looks like, and here is how to walk in it.

The blessed man is described first by negatives: he does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers. There is a progression here—walking, standing, sitting—suggesting the gradual entanglement of one who begins to compromise. The righteous man avoids this drift entirely.

His positive characteristic is delight in the law of the Lord, meditating on it day and night. Meditation is not the absence of thought but the filling of thought with God's word. The result: he is like a tree planted by streams of water—not a tree that happens to find water, but one deliberately planted where the source is sure and constant.
psa.1.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

psa.23.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Psalm 23
psa.23.text:
The Twenty-third Psalm is the pearl of the Psalter. It is the expression of a soul at rest in God's care—not a soul free from trouble, but a soul at peace in the midst of it. 'The Lord is my shepherd'—this is the most personal of claims. Not 'a shepherd' or 'our shepherd' but 'my shepherd.' The covenant relationship is individual.

The sheep's contentment is entirely dependent on the shepherd's competence. 'I shall not want' is not a claim of personal sufficiency but a declaration of trust in the Shepherd's provision. Green pastures and still waters speak of both refreshment and restoration—what is given freely and what is recovered after loss.

The valley of the shadow of death is not avoided in this psalm; it is walked through. But 'through' implies an exit. And the Shepherd is present in the valley: 'You are with me.' The rod and staff—instruments of correction and rescue—are sources of comfort, not fear.
psa.23.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

psa.51.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Psalm 51
psa.51.text:
This is the great penitential psalm, written after Nathan the prophet came to David following his sin with Bathsheba. It is the anatomy of true repentance: honest acknowledgment of sin, understanding of its true nature, and cry for renewal.

'Have mercy on me, O God'—the psalm begins with an appeal to God's character, not to David's merit. Steadfast love and abundant mercy are the foundation of his plea. He does not come bargaining; he comes begging.

'Against you, you only, have I sinned'—this does not deny the harm done to Bathsheba and Uriah, but recognizes that all sin is ultimately against God. Sin is not merely a violation of social standards but a transgression against the holy God.

'Create in me a clean heart'—the word 'create' is the same used in Genesis 1. David is asking for a miracle, not a renovation. He knows his heart cannot be reformed by effort; it must be recreated by grace.
psa.51.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

mat.5.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Matthew 5 (Sermon on the Mount)
mat.5.text:
Our Lord opens the Sermon on the Mount with eight beatitudes—declarations of blessedness over conditions the world considers unfortunate. Each beatitude begins with 'Blessed' (makarios), meaning deeply happy, fortunate, to be envied.

The poor in spirit: those who feel their own spiritual bankruptcy, who know they have no righteousness of their own. The kingdom belongs to such. This is where the Christian life begins—not with achievement but with the acknowledgment of need.

Those who mourn: grief over sin, over the state of the world, over one's own spiritual poverty. The promise is comfort—not the elimination of grief, but the divine presence within it.

The meek shall inherit the earth: meekness is not weakness but strength under control. Moses was called the meekest man on earth, yet he confronted Pharaoh. The meek are those who have submitted their wills to God and so are free from the anxiety of self-promotion.
mat.5.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

jhn.3.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on John 3
jhn.3.text:
Nicodemus came to Jesus by night—perhaps for privacy, perhaps from the mixture of curiosity and caution that marks many sincere seekers. Jesus does not address his compliment but goes immediately to his need: 'You must be born again.'

The new birth is not a self-improvement program or a moral reformation. It is a new beginning at the deepest level of human nature. 'Born of water and Spirit'—born of the washing that the Spirit accomplishes, the renewal of the inner man that makes one fit for the kingdom of God.

John 3:16 is rightly called the gospel in miniature. Four things: the source (God's love), the extent (the world), the provision (His only Son), and the terms (belief). The offer is not to the good or the deserving but to 'whoever believes.' The threatened consequence is not suffering but perishing—the loss of the life that God intended for humanity.
jhn.3.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

rom.8.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Romans 8
rom.8.text:
Romans 8 is the Mount Everest of the New Testament—the fullest expression of the Christian's security in Christ. It opens with 'no condemnation' and closes with 'no separation.' Between these two great pillars, the whole of the Christian life is secured.

The chapter moves from the Spirit's work in our daily lives (walking by the Spirit, not the flesh) to our adoption as children of God (crying 'Abba, Father') to the groaning of creation awaiting redemption, to the intercession of the Spirit in our weakness, to the great chain of God's saving purpose (foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, glorification), to the triumphant conclusion: nothing—nothing—shall separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.

'All things work together for good' (v.28): this is not a promise that all things are pleasant, but that in the hands of a sovereign, loving God, nothing is wasted. The trial, the loss, the delay—all are being woven into a purpose beyond our sight.
rom.8.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)

rev.21.title: Matthew Henry's Commentary on Revelation 21
rev.21.text:
The vision of the new heaven and new earth is the culmination of the whole biblical story. It is not a return to the garden of Eden but something greater—a city, the New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven. The movement is not upward escape but downward renewal: God coming to dwell with His people.

'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes'—this is a personal and tender act. Not 'tears will no longer exist' but 'He will wipe them.' The great God stoops to minister to the grief of His children. Death, mourning, crying, pain—all former things—shall be no more.

'Behold, I am making all things new'—not 'all new things' but all things renewed. Creation is not discarded; it is restored and glorified. The promise reaches its fulfilment: the dwelling place of God is with man.
rev.21.source: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (Public Domain)
